nameStory: This critically endangered sea turtle is named after Richard Kemp, a fisherman and naturalist from Key West, Florida, who first submitted a specimen to science in 1880. The 'ridley' part of the name comes from the genus Lepidochelys, which includes two species of sea turtles known for their relatively small size and distinctive nesting behaviors.
description: Kemp's ridley is the world's smallest and rarest sea turtle, with adults typically reaching about 2 feet long and weighing 75-100 pounds. These critically endangered turtles have a nearly circular, grayish-green shell and are primarily found in the Gulf of Mexico, though they occasionally venture into Atlantic waters off New England. Their small size, broad head, and distinctive shell shape make them unique among sea turtles. Unfortunately, fewer than 10,000 nesting females remain in the wild.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Nearly circular carapace (top shell) that's broader than it is long, giving it an almost round appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Smallest of all sea turtles, with adults typically 24-28 inches long - noticeably smaller than other sea turtle species

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to dark gray carapace with a lighter-colored, yellowish plastron (bottom shell)

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Large, triangular head relative to body size with a hooked beak and powerful jaw muscles

idTips.label: Flippers
idTips.description: Two claws on each front flipper, which feel leathery and strong to the touch

habitat: In New England waters, Kemp's ridleys are found in shallow coastal areas, bays, and nearshore waters where they feed on crabs and other bottom-dwelling creatures. They prefer sandy or muddy bottoms where blue crabs and other prey are abundant. These turtles are typically found in warmer months when Gulf Stream currents carry them northward into our region.

seasonality.spring: Kemp's ridleys begin appearing in New England waters as temperatures warm, often found in shallow bays feeding on crabs.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings, when juveniles may be found in eelgrass beds and adults in deeper coastal waters.
seasonality.fall: Most active period before migration, but vulnerable to cold-stunning events during sudden temperature drops.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England waters; those that remain risk cold-stunning and may strand on beaches, requiring rescue.

funFact: Kemp's ridley females engage in one of nature's most spectacular synchronized events called an 'arribada' - thousands of females come ashore to nest on the same beach on the same day, but this only happens on one primary beach in the entire world: Rancho Nuevo in Mexico.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with juvenile loggerhead sea turtles, but Kemp's ridley has a more circular shell shape and smaller adult size. Remember: 'Kemp's is compact' - the round shell and smaller size are dead giveaways.
contextualKnowledge: Kemp's ridley is listed as Critically Endangered under the Endangered Species Act, making it illegal to harass, harm, or handle these turtles. If you encounter one, especially a stranded individual, contact local marine wildlife authorities immediately as it may need medical attention.
compareHints: While Kemp's ridley is the only Lepidochelys species found in New England waters, it differs from its cousin the olive ridley (found in Pacific waters) by having a grayer coloration and slightly more heart-shaped shell. Compared to other sea turtles in New England, Kemp's ridley is distinguished by its notably round shell shape and smaller size - loggerheads are much larger with more elongated shells, while green sea turtles have more pronounced growth rings on their shell plates.
